title: Wild cosmic ducks
caption: Part of the Wild Duck Cluster, Messier 11, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 11 · constellation Scutum · about 6000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, P. Dobbie et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Stars fill this Hubble view of part of Messier 11, an open cluster found in Scutum, the Shield, in the southern sky. It is nicknamed the Wild Duck Cluster because its brightest stars form a V shape a little like ducks flying in formation.

Messier 11 is among the richest and most compact open clusters known. By studying its brightest, hottest main-sequence stars, astronomers estimate its age at roughly 220 million years. Open clusters usually hold fewer and younger stars than globular clusters, and this one fits the pattern. At its center are many blue stars, the hottest and youngest of its few thousand members.

Open clusters also do not last as long. Their stars are more widely spaced, so gravity holds them together less tightly, and stronger pulls from outside can drag them away. Messier 11 is likely to break up within a few million years as other objects nearby pull its stars off one at a time.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.69 x 2.59 arcminutes) and distance (6000 light years), the frame spans roughly 4.7 × 4.5 light-years. Its light set out about 6,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the cluster through an ultraviolet and a visible filter. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the human eye, which could never see this part of the data directly.

explore: Main-sequence stars are those in the long, steady middle of their lives, fusing hydrogen in their cores. Messier 11 lies about 6000 light-years away.
